questions.q: What does the --code-coverage flag on sf apex run test require alongside it?
questions.explain: The CLI requires --result-format whenever --code-coverage is used, so it knows how to present the coverage figures.

questions.q: Which --test-level value runs every test in the org except tests from installed managed and unlocked packages, and is the default Salesforce applies to production deployments that include Apex?
questions.explain: RunLocalTests is the default for production deployments containing Apex, and deliberately excludes managed/unlocked package tests you don't own.

questions.q: What is the minimum Apex code coverage percentage required to deploy classes and triggers to a production org?
questions.explain: Salesforce enforces a 75% org-wide Apex coverage floor (with per-class/trigger minimums too) before allowing a production deployment of Apex.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a CI pipeline should always pass --test-level explicitly rather than leaving it unspecified?
options: Because deployments to sandboxes and Developer Edition orgs run zero tests by default, so an unspecified level can silently mean no coverage was ever checked
Because the CLI will refuse to run without it
Because --test-level is required to authenticate to the org
Because it has no effect either way
questions.explain: Non-production orgs default to running no tests unless told otherwise — leaving --test-level out of a shared pipeline risks a deploy that silently never checked coverage at all.

questions.q: What does the --detailed-coverage flag add when used with human-readable test output?
options: It deletes all failing tests from the report
It breaks coverage down per individual test method, not just per class
It disables code coverage checking entirely
It automatically deploys the code after tests pass
questions.explain: --detailed-coverage shows coverage at the test-method level, useful for pinpointing exactly which lines a suite still misses.
